messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance Sampling doubts, reg.
messages.body_plain:
A.K.

Density of groups is calculated for the Distance for Windows software by treating each group, regardless of size, as if it was a group of size one.  In other words, the software computes the estimated number of groups in the sampled region and divides this number by the size of the sampled region.  The density of groups in the sampled region is assumed equal to the density of groups in the entire study area as the sampled region is assumed representative of the entire study area.

The issue of size bias adjustment is treated in a lecture and exercise available in our online distance sampling training materials.  As a beginner, I suggest you visit all the chapters of the training materials
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
but particularly Chapter 5 where the lecture and exercise on size bias can be found
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk

> Dear all,
>
> I am a beginner with distance sampling and DISTANCE software. I want to ask to the group members a few doubts that I had in my mind.
>
> 1. How the group density is calculated in the DISTANCE?
>
> 2. How does the DISTANCE software deal with the group size effect, It corrects the size bias when the larger groups are detected at long-distance?
>
> 3. My concern is that if the larger groups are detected at the nearer distances and smaller groups are getting detected at the farther distances. Then, how does distance sampling theory and DISTANCE software deal with this size bias?
>
> Could you please give me insight on this?
> Thanks
>
> Regards

messages.subject: Live distance sampling training workshop 17-28 February 2020, Registration now open
messages.subject_clean: Live distance sampling training workshop 17-28 February 2020, Registration now open
messages.body_plain:
Interactive introductory distance sampling training

The University of St Andrews has been training people in design and analysis of distance sampling studies for decades.  Perhaps you've wanted to attend but could not get permission for travel to Scotland or the scheduling of workshops in August conflicted with your field work. 👨‍🌾

We are offering the training workshop in 10 two-hour blocks in late February.  You will be invited to interact in short lectures on distance sampling principles. 👩‍🎓 Exercises analysing data sets in R will reinforce those principles and the lecturer will be available to assist during the practical session via screen sharing.  The block will conclude with a summary of the exercise and question/answer session for both lecture and exercise. 💻  You can participate in polls during the workshop to assess your comprehension of topics discussed. 🤔

The workshop will be delivered using Zoom web conferencing software along with R-Studio "in the cloud"☁️; both free software tools.  You will need accounts for both pieces of software. I encourage you to experiment with Zoom (at https://zoom.us) and https://rstudio.cloud before the course begins. 👩‍💻

Registration for the first two offering of this training each filled within a week of advertisement.  Persons on the wait list from earlier offerings have already filled some of the available places.  I suggest you register and pay without delay.

Important details:

    Workshop dates and time: 17-28 February 2020; 1600-1800 UK time (1100-1300 EST, 0800-1000 PST) 🕰️
    Registration deadline: 07 February 2020📅
    Enrolment limit: 10 - several participants from the wait list have already registered
    Cost: 170 British pounds (roughly 205USD at current exchange rates)💵

    What is included: Lectures, exercises, code, data all available online📃

Further details are available at the CREEM website:

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-live-online-workshops/

At this page you will find a link to the St Andrews online shop where you a) register and b) make payment.

Feel free to contact me with questions.  This will be the last interactive training St Andrews will conduct for the winter 2019-2020.  Watch for the next round of offerings in autumn 2020. 🍂

The interactive workshops do not replace face-to-face distance sampling workshops that will be held in August 2020.  Information regarding all distance sampling workshops can be found at

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/workshops/

--

messages.body_plain:
Interactive introductory distance sampling training

Registration closes in little more than a week for this web-based training.  There are a few places remaining.  Reply to me if you have questions.

The University of St Andrews has been training people in design and analysis of distance sampling studies for decades. Distance sampling methods for estimating animal abundance is one of the most widely used methods in not only terrestrial systems but also marine mammal 🐋 investigations where assessment of marine mammal populations is difficult because imperfect detectability.  Perhaps you've wanted to attend but could not get permission for travel to Scotland or the scheduling of workshops in August conflicted with your field work. 👨‍🌾

We are offering the training workshop in 10 two-hour blocks in late February.  You will be invited to interact in short lectures on distance sampling principles. 👩‍🎓 Exercises analysing data sets in R will reinforce those principles and the lecturer will be available to assist during the practical session via screen sharing.  The block will conclude with a summary of the exercise and question/answer session for both lecture and exercise. 💻  You can participate in polls during the workshop to assess your comprehension of topics discussed. 🤔

The workshop will be delivered using Zoom web conferencing software along with R-Studio "in the cloud"☁️; both free software tools.  You will need accounts for both pieces of software. I encourage you to experiment with Zoom (at https://zoom.us) and https://rstudio.cloud before the course begins. 👩‍💻

Important details:

    Workshop dates and time: 17-28 February 2020; 1600-1800 UK time (1100-1300 EST, 0800-1000 PST) 🕰️
    Registration deadline: 07 February 2020📅
    Enrolment limit: 10 - several participants from the wait list have already registered
    Cost: 170 British pounds (roughly 205USD at current exchange rates)💵
    What is included: Lectures, exercises, code, data all available online📃

Further details are available at the CREEM website:

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-live-online-workshops/

At this page you will find a link to the St Andrews online shop where you a) register and b) make payment.

Feel free to contact me with questions.  This will be the last interactive training St Andrews will conduct for the winter 2019-2020.  Watch for the next round of offerings in autumn 2020. 🍂

The interactive workshops do not replace face-to-face distance sampling workshops that will be held in August 2020.  Information regarding all distance sampling workshops can be found at

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/workshops/

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Group size and ds
messages.body_plain:
Graham

Rather than re-enter your data, it still seems as if the distribution of perpendicular distances is not going to be monotonically decreasing.  The smallest perpendicular distance i see is 36.  That makes it unlikely that detectability on the transect is perfect.  Make a plot of the fitted detection function (as I showed in the previous email), I predict the data still suggests that the best fit to the observed data is a horizontal detection function implying that detectability is one on the transect line and does not decline as distance from the transect increases.  A histogram of perpendicular distances below 600m (detections beyond this distance likely have little information about the shape of the detection function at very small distances) is attached.  It shows that detectability does not seem to decrease as a function of distance from the transect as distance sampling assumes (not the single detection <50m).

I do not think it is an issue related to group size, but rather observed distances from the transect do not conform to the assumptions of distance sampling.  Do you think you detect all animals located on the transect?  I suggest reviewing the search procedure in the field so as to ensure detectability is highest (perfect) on the transect, and declining as a function of perpendicular distance.

Eric Rexstad

messages.subject: {Disarmed} Reanalysis of your sheep data
messages.body_plain:
Graham

In the cold light of day, I have entered your data and performed a more thorough distance sampling analysis, rather than concentrating only upon the perpendicular distances.

Note I also changed the size of the study area to 1 km^2, simply to make the values of abundance larger, I did not perform truncation, which I would likely do in a more complete analysis.  The field named "object" is extraneous and I have removed it.  It would be sequential numbering of detections, so not needed for the transects on which no detections were made.

In any event, I include my code:

library(Distance)

setwd("C:/Users/erexs/OneDrive/Desktop")

sheep <- read.csv(file="upton2.txt",header=FALSE,

                  colClasses=c("factor", "integer", "integer",

                               "numeric", "integer",

                               "numeric"))

names(sheep) <- c("Region.Label", "Area",

                  "Sample.Label", "Effort",

                  "size", "distance")

estimate.with.size <- ds(sheep)

size.drop <- sheep

size.drop$size <- NULL

estimate.without.size <- ds(size.drop)

summary(estimate.with.size)

summary(estimate.without.size)

messages.subject: Cluster sampling design with point transects
messages.subject_clean: Cluster sampling design with point transects
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Following is a question related to cluster sampling design for which I would like to ask your advice since I was not able to find anything similar to our situation in the design sections of general distance sampling books (Buckland et al. 1993; Strindberg et al. 2004; Buckland et al. 2015) and specialised primate sections (Peres, 1999; Buckland et al. 2010; Ross and Reeve 2011).

Context

I have the opportunity to join a team currently conducting a bird survey in a forested national park in the Philippines, in order to conduct a separate macaque population survey while benefiting from their logistics. This is in an area where we know little about the primates. However, this situation also means that my survey is restricted by their plan, and I am having doubts about the most efficient design to adopt within their conditions.

Planning

The survey will be conducted from bivouac camps in the park, during week-long expeditions comprising 2 camps each.
For the location of the camps, they made a grid of 2,5 km-wide squares in the middle of which the camps will be set. The blue dots represent the camp locations which were randomly chosen, yet I will only be able to access 8-10 of them in the time of the study (4-5 expeditions). The camps visited are still to be confirmed, but chosen indenpendantly from the terrain.
In each camp we will stay 2 days surveying points equally spaced (every 250m) along 1 km line transects spreading out from the camp (starting at 250m from the camp).

As of today, I plan to follow their methodology, i.e. doing point counts every 250m on 1 km transect outward from the camps (in a cross pattern). Yet, I wonder if this design will allow to draw inferences to estimate reliable density and abundance for the whole park. According to Buckland et al. (2015:16) “If the separation of neighbouring points on the same line is less than the separation of neighbouring points on different lines, then this should be treated as cluster sampling, where each line represents one cluster of points.”

My main question is the following:

Is there a problem to consider the 2 or more lines of points departing 250m from a same camp (to avoid human disturbance bias and overlapping) as independent sampling units? Would using this sampling design above respect the principles of survey design?

Considering the different point transects from one camp together as one sampling unit would maybe produce data-rich samples but insufficient in number (8-10) for adequate replication, right?

Thanks for your help,

Gaspard

Ps: please pardon the lengthy message. The attached grid has been designed due to the absence of a trail system and accidented terrain making travel difficult.

messages.body_plain:
Gaspard, I can’t see the attached image, but I am afraid that you would need to consider each camp as an independent sampling unit.  Whether 8-10 is sufficient replication depends on how heterogeneous density is.  If the environment is relatively homogeneous, that might be fine.  If not, your analysis will still be valid, but confidence intervals may be wide.  You’ll have the advantage of lots of data per camp, so that you should at least have fairly precise data from each camp.

You should consider a more model-based approach.  For example you can fit a density surface model using the dsm engine of distance, and hence estimate density through the park by that means.

Steve

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of gaspard van hamme
Sent: 31 January 2020 10:16
To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [distance-sampling] Cluster sampling design using Point transects

Hi all,

I would like to ask your advice concerning cluster sampling. I am novice to distance sampling and was not able to find anything similar to our situation in the design sections of general distance sampling books (Buckland et al. 1993; Strindberg et al. 2004; Buckland et al. 2015) and specialised primate sections (Peres 1999; Buckland et al. 2010; Ross and Reeve 2011).

Context

I have the opportunity to join a team currently conducting a bird survey in a forested national park in the Philippines, in order to conduct a separate macaque population survey while benefiting from their logistics. This is in an area where we know little about the primates. However, this situation also means that my survey is restricted by their plan, and I am doubting about the most efficient design to adopt within their conditions.

Planning

·      The survey will be conducted from bivouac camps in the park, during week-long expeditions comprising 2 camps each.

·      For the location of the camps, they made a grid of 2,5 km-wide squares in the middle of which the camps will be set (see attached). The blue dots represent the camp locations which were randomly chosen, yet I will only be able to access 8-10 of them in the time of the study (4-5 expeditions). The camps visited are still to be confirmed, but chosen indenpendently from the terrain or animal distribution.

·      In each camp we will stay 2 days surveying the grid square.

As As of today, I plan to follow their methodology, i.e. doing point counts every 250m on 1 km transects (2 or 3 per camp) spreading out from the camps (in a cross pattern). Yet, I wonder if this design will allow to draw inferences to estimate reliable density and abundance for the whole park.

According to Buckland et al. (2015:16) “If the separation of neighbouring points on the same line is less than the separation of neighbouring points on different lines, then this should be treated as cluster sampling, where each line represents one cluster of points.”
Is there a problem to consider the 2 or more lines of points departing 250m from a same camp (to avoid human disturbance bias and overlapping) as independent sampling units?
Would using this sampling design respect the principles of survey design?

It seems that considering the different point transects from one camp together as one sampling unit would produce data-rich samples but insufficient in number (8-10) for adequate replication.

Thanks for your help,

Gaspard

Ps: please pardon the lengthy message. The attached grid has been designed due to the absence of a trail system and accidented terrain making travel difficult. The grid covers most of the park's territory which does not reach the coast.

·      Buckland, S. T., A. J. Plumptre, L. Thomas, and E. A. Rexstad (2010). Design and analysis of line transect surveys for primates. International Journal of Primatology 31, 833–847.

·      Buckland, S. T., D. R. Anderson, K. P. Burnham, and J. L. Laake (1993). Distance Sampling: Estimating Abundance of Biological Populations. London: Chapman and Hall.

·      Buckland, S. T., Rexstad, E. A., Marques, T. A., & Oedekoven, C. S. (2015). Distance sampling: Methods and applications (1st ed.). Cham, Switzerland: Springer.

·      Peres, C.A. (1999). General guidelines for standardizing line-transect surveys of tropical forest primates. Neotropical primates 7(1):11-16.

·      Ross, C., and Reeve, N. (2011). Survey and census methods: population distribution and density. In: Field and Laboratory Methods in Primatology, 111–132.

·      Strindberg, S., S. T. Buckland, and L. Thomas (2004). Design of distance sampling surveys and geographic information systems. pp. 190–228 in S. T. Buckland, D. R. Anderson, K. P. Burnham, J. L. Laake, D. L. Borchers, and L. Thomas (Eds.), Advanced Distance Sampling. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
